subject: Economics
topic: Monetary policy and RBI tools — mixed tiers
description: Repo, reverse repo, MPC, CRR, SLR, OMO, MSF, inflation targeting framework

questions.stem: The 'repo rate' is the rate at which the:

options.option_text: RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities

questions.explanation: Repo (repurchase) — RBI lends overnight to banks against G-Sec collateral; banks 'sell with a repurchase agreement'. Repo is the policy rate; sets the floor for short-term interest rates. As of Apr 2025: Repo = 6.00% (after a 25 bp cut in Apr-25 MPC). Reverse repo — RBI borrows from banks (currently 3.35%, rarely used since SDF was introduced in Apr 2022). SDF — Standing Deposit Facility (3.50% in Apr 2025) is the lower-bound; MSF — Marginal Standing Facility (6.25%) is the upper-bound. Bank Rate (now aligned to MSF). LAF (Liquidity Adjustment Facility) corridor: SDF (lower) – Repo (mid) – MSF (upper).

questions.stem: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) in India was formed under the amended RBI Act, 1934. Its composition is:

options.option_text: 6 members — 3 from RBI (incl. Governor as Chair, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer) + 3 external members appointed by the Centre
All members from the Finance Ministry

questions.explanation: MPC — created in 2016 by an amendment to the RBI Act 1934. 6 members: (1) RBI Governor (ex-officio Chairperson, casting vote in case of tie); (2) Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy; (3) one RBI officer nominated by Central Board; (4-6) three external members appointed by the Centre (typically economists). Term of external members — 4 years, non-renewable. Decisions by majority; if 3-3 tie, Governor's casting vote. Meets at least 4 times a year (usually 6 — every 2 months). Mandate: maintain headline CPI inflation at 4% ± 2% (i.e., 2-6% band) — 'flexible inflation targeting'; review every 5 years (current term till Mar 2026).

options.option_text: Loans banks must give to priority sectors
The proportion of a bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that must be kept with the RBI in cash, earning no interest
Foreign exchange reserves of the RBI

questions.explanation: CRR — % of NDTL kept as cash with RBI; no interest paid. Currently 4% (Apr 2025). Reducing CRR — releases liquidity to banks (more lending capacity, expansionary). SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio) — % of NDTL kept in liquid assets (G-Sec, gold, cash with the bank itself); currently 18% (Apr 2025). Earns interest. Quantitative tools of monetary policy: CRR, SLR, OMO (Open Market Operations — RBI buys/sells G-Sec to manage liquidity), LAF, MSF. Qualitative tools: margin requirements, moral suasion, credit rationing. CRR floor was earlier 3% (statutory), but the floor was removed by amendment.

questions.stem: When the RBI BUYS government securities from banks in the open market, it is called:

options.option_text: Open Market Purchase (expansionary — injects liquidity into banking system)

questions.explanation: OMO (Open Market Operations) — RBI's tool for managing liquidity. PURCHASE of G-Sec from banks = pays banks → liquidity in system rises (expansionary). SALE of G-Sec to banks = banks pay RBI → liquidity falls (contractionary). RBI uses OMOs to fine-tune short-term liquidity, especially around tax-payment cycles or festive demand. Operation Twist — variant where RBI simultaneously buys long-term G-Sec and sells short-term G-Sec to flatten the yield curve (used during 2019-20). VRR (Variable Rate Repo) and VRRR (Variable Rate Reverse Repo) — variable-rate auctions for liquidity management.

questions.stem: RBI's primary inflation target under the flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework is:

options.option_text: Headline CPI (Consumer Price Index, combined) at 4% ± 2% (i.e., a 2-6% band)

questions.explanation: FIT framework — operationalised by the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) → MPC Act amendments (2016). Target: 4% ± 2% headline CPI (combined). Set by the Centre in consultation with RBI; reviewed every 5 years (current target valid till 31 Mar 2026). FAILURE — if CPI is outside the 2-6% band for 3 consecutive quarters, RBI must submit a report to the Centre explaining reasons + remedial action + expected return-to-target horizon. (RBI failed in 2022 — submitted such a report for the first time.) WPI (Wholesale Price Index) — was the main inflation measure pre-2014; RBI now uses CPI as the headline target. Core inflation = CPI excluding food & fuel.

questions.stem: The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) was introduced in 2011 as:

options.option_text: An emergency overnight borrowing window for banks at a rate higher than the repo rate (currently repo + 25 bp)

questions.explanation: MSF — introduced 9 May 2011. Banks can borrow OVERNIGHT from RBI by dipping into their SLR holdings (up to 2% of NDTL — increased to 3% temporarily during COVID). Rate = repo + 25 bp (currently 6.25% in Apr 2025 with repo at 6.00%). Used as the upper bound of the LAF corridor. MSF is a 'penalty' window for emergency liquidity; banks rarely use it heavily — it's a signalling tool. Bank Rate is now aligned with MSF. The corridor (lower bound = SDF since 2022; upper bound = MSF) helps RBI keep call money rates close to the repo rate.

questions.stem: When the RBI INCREASES the repo rate, the typical (textbook) effect on the economy is:

options.option_text: Borrowing becomes costlier → demand cools → inflation expected to ease over time (contractionary)

questions.explanation: Repo hike (contractionary monetary policy): banks face higher cost of borrowing from RBI → pass-through to lending rates (home, auto, business loans cost more) → loan demand falls → consumer + business spending eases → demand-side inflation reduces. Lag — typically 6-9 months for full transmission. Side-effects: GDP growth tends to slow (inflation-growth tradeoff); savings yields rise (good for senior citizens); rupee may strengthen marginally (higher rates attract foreign investment). REVERSE — repo cut: stimulus, cheaper credit, growth-friendly. RBI's stance shifts from 'accommodative' (cut bias) to 'neutral' to 'tight' (hike bias) depending on inflation-growth balance. April 2025 — 25 bp cut, stance maintained at 'neutral'.
